## Design

### 2026-10-12 – Here is the detailed report of the work done in this 4-hour session, focused on bringing the PCB from KiCad into Fusion 360 and building the physical base of our enclosure.

**4.5h**

Here is the detailed report of the work done in this 4-hour session, focused on bringing the PCB from KiCad into Fusion 360 and building the physical base of our enclosure.

Phase 1: PCB Import and Project Study
I started the project by importing the .step file directly from the KiCad PCB into Fusion 360. With the 3D model in the workspace, the first task was to analyze the critical points, focusing especially on the four 2.8 mm diameter mounting holes.

![WhatsApp Image 2026-10-12 at 14.32.18](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/T4VNKFYucNS23P2qnOKuArH2j1qOxcfx/b34ad8c24541d60686837e679f5429eb7c4c6ad45290937a24c5288377e783f1.jpg)

(Drag and drop your first screenshot here - Initial 3D view of the PCB)

To map and ensure concentricity between the board holes and our future case, I rotated the camera to view the bottom part. I used the P (Project) shortcut to copy the exact geometry of the mounting holes and started marking them on a new Sketch.

![WhatsApp Image 2026-10-12 at 14.43.34](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/T4VNKFYucNS23P2qnOKuArH2j1qOxcfx/94e751374381aef367ed002dc56aed0e417733ce63cbb8ad377ad0dccc1baf25.jpg)

(Drag and drop your screenshot here - Using the P key looking at the bottom of the PCB)

Phase 2: The Extrusion and Mapping Challenge
With the holes projected, I used the Circle tool (C) in the sketch. I drew a circular ring at each of the four points: the outer ring with Ø5.5 mm and the inner one with Ø2.8 mm (the ideal size for M3 screws to bite directly into the plastic).

(Drag and drop your screenshot here - 2D drawing of the standoffs)

Next came the "Eureka moment": making my first 3D extrusion! I exited the sketch and, using the E (Extrude) key, I pulled the "ring" of the first standoff by 4.0 mm, creating the first support cylinder.

(Drag and drop your screenshot here - The first 3D standoff)

The "Inversion" Riddle (Challenges Faced)
After making the standoffs, I created a 138 x 113 mm rectangular sketch to make the "floor" (bottom) of the case. This is where the process got complicated: after the 2.0 mm extrusion, I noticed the solid was generated upwards, "swallowing" the PCB and components like the ESP32, and the holes were completely covered.

![WhatsApp Image 2026-10-12 at 14.56.30](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/T4VNKFYucNS23P2qnOKuArH2j1qOxcfx/c7a574560675586daf375deab8978118913a607c293297cc7d69965c6820634e.jpg)
After a few hours of trying, getting lost in the camera views, and adjusting the project, I identified the error. I edited the feature in the timeline, inverted the extrusion direction to -2.0 mm, and deselected the center holes. This pushed the base downwards, left the standoffs on the correct side, and kept the 2.8 mm through-holes perfectly open!

(Drag and drop your screenshot here - Base fixed with correct standoffs)

Phase 3: Refinement and Top Cover with Autodesk Assistant
In the final stage of this session, I relied on the Autodesk Assistant to model the Top Cover and its tolerances. We discovered that the actual physical board didn't follow the standard 19.05 mm keyboard pitch, but rather a more compact 15.09 mm layout.

The Assistant helped align the cover, create the nine 14x14 mm Cherry MX cutouts, the OLED window (12x26 mm in portrait mode), and project the new mounting bosses perfectly aligned with our base.

(Drag and drop your screenshot here - Top cover with the cutouts)

We finished by applying a 0.25 mm clearance (offset) between the cover and the base for a smooth assembly after printing, along with 2.0 mm and 3.0 mm fillets on the outer edges for an ergonomic finish.
